Title: Co-occurring EGFR and BRAF mutations in a patient with lung adenocarcinoma: A case report
PMID: 
Authors: 

ABSTRACT
Vrafmurine sarcoma viral oncogene homolog B (BRAF) mutations, including both V600E and non‐V600E variants, are infrequent in non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), representing approximately 2% of lung adenocarcinomas. Activated BRAF mutations are regarded as an underappreciated oncogenic driver in NSCLC, typically occurring in a mutually exclusive manner with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations, as well as ALK and ROS1 rearrangements. In recent years, advancements in multiple‐gene panel testing have demonstrated that EGFR mutations and BRAF mutations can coexist. Notably, the secondary BRAF V600E mutation has been identified as one of the mechanisms contributing to resistance against EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) in EGFR‐mutated lung adenocarcinomas. However, the role of co‐occurring BRAF mutations and associated treatment strategies in patients with EGFR mutations has not been thoroughly investigated. Additionally, the profile of adverse events related to combination therapy has not been previously evaluated. This case report presents a patient with co‐occurring EGFR and BRAF mutations who demonstrated a sustained response and tolerance to adverse events when treated with a combination of Osimertinib, Trametinib, and Dabrafenib.

1.1. Case Presentation
In April 2023, a 65‐year‐old male patient presented to our hospital with a complaint of sputum production. The symptoms had persisted for 1 month and were not accompanied by chest tightness or pain. The patient has a smoking history exceeding 20 years and reports no family history of genetic disorders. Physical examination revealed a palpable mass in the right chest wall, measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter, characterized by its firmness and indistinct borders relative to the surrounding tissue. Additionally, an enlarged lymph node was palpated in the right axilla, also measuring around 2.5 cm in diameter. Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest demonstrated a mass located within the right chest wall as well as irregular nodules present in the upper lobe of the right lung. Subsequently, positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) revealed positive lesions in the right chest wall, the upper lobe of the right lung, and several lymph nodes in the mediastinum, axillae, and supraclavicular region (Figure 1). The standard uptake value for these sites was above 2.5. A puncture biopsy of the right chest wall mass and the right axillary lymph nodes was performed on April 24, 2023, and the pathologic results suggested that the tumor of the right chest wall originated from the lung. A CT‐guided needle lung puncture biopsy of the upper lobe of the right lung was conducted on April 27, 2023, with the pathology showing moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma (Figure 2). Furthermore, genetic testing for common lung cancers using next‐generation sequencing (NGS) revealed a double mutation of EGFR‐19 del and BRAF V600E (Figure 3).
In accordance with the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC)/Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) 8th edition Tumor Node Metastasis (TNM) staging classification, the patient was initially diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma (CT2aN3M1b IVA), chest wall metastasis, and lymph node metastasis in the mediastinum, axillae, and supraclavicular regions. Referring to the 2023 Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology (CSCO) guidelines and National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines, targeted therapy is preferred for stage IV non‐small cell lung cancer with EGFR or BRAF mutations. Considering that the patient in this case had a primary EGFR and BRAF double mutation, we tried to select a multi‐drug combination therapy. The treatment plan was formulated as follows: (1) oral targeted drug Osimertinib mesylate 80 mg once daily (qd); (2) oral Trametinib 2 mg once daily (qd); (3) oral Dabrafenib mesylate 250 mg twice daily (bid). The patient was treated with Osimertinib in combination with Trametinib and Dabrafenib from May 18, 2023, and follow‐up every 2 months to assess efficacy.
The follow‐up CT reexamination conducted on June 15, 2023, indicated a total reduction in target lesion diameters of 30.9%. The efficacy was evaluated as partial remission (PR) according to RESIST 1.1 guidelines. At subsequent follow‐ups, the efficacy of the treatment was sustained in PR. During the course of treatment, the patient experienced low fever, intermittent diarrhea, and grade I‐II liver function abnormality, which improved after symptomatic treatment. Due to the patient's persistent low‐grade fever, the dose of dabrafenib was reduced to 75 mg qd. By the time of the follow‐up in June 2024, the patient's PFS had already been more than 13 months, and the treatment did not show any serious adverse reactions.
